newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FOCUS - HK airlines cancel flights after problems.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - HK airlines cancel flights after problems.

text.p: Hong Kong's two airlines said they suspended a total of 15 Airbus Industrie A330-300 aircraft on Saturday, leading to the cancellation of 25 flights, as a result of concerns about their Rolls-Royce engines.
Cathay Pacific Airways Ltd suspended 11 aircraft and Hong Kong Dragon Airlines Ltd (Dragonair) suspended four, both because of questions about the reliability of their Rolls-Royce Trent 700 engines.
By contrast, Indonesia's flag carrier Garuda Indonesia said on Saturday it intended to continue flying its six A330-300 aircraft which have the same engine types.

The suspensions followed the failure of a Trent 700 engine on a Dragonair A330 on Friday. Flight KA/MH061 from Hong Kong made an emergency landing on one of its two engines at Subic Bay in the Philippines after developing engine trouble en route to Kota Kinabalu in Malaysia.
It was the latest in a series of single-engine landings by Airbus A330-300 planes from the two airlines.
Cathay, the territory's flag carrier, said it had cancelled 18 flights, or 15 percent of all its services, on Saturday. Some other flights were being rescheduled.

The cancelled flights included those from Hong Kong to Jakarta, Singapore, Seoul, Kansai, Taipei and Perth, and to the territory from Taipei, Singapore, Penang, Jakarta, Tokyo, Bangkok and Cairns. A flight from Bangkok to Colombo had also been cancelled.
Most of the passengers on the cancelled flights were put on other flights, a Cathay spokeswoman told Reuters.
The carrier did not ground its four Boeing Co B-777 aircraft, which are powered by another type of Rolls-Royce Trent engine.
"There's a big differentiation between the two engine types. There is absolutely no connection. They are completely different engines," the Cathay spokeswoman said.
A spokeswoman from Dragonair said the carrier had cancelled seven flights and rescheduled eight on Saturday. Passengers from the cancelled flights were being booked on other airlines.
She gave no further information on the affected flights.
Anthony Philips, another spokesman for Dragonair, told Reuters the suspended aircraft mainly served routes to Beijing, Shanghai, Kaohsiung and Xiamen.
The Dragonair spokeswoman said the suspension also led to the downgrading of seats for some passengers.
Thousands of passengers were believed to be affected by the aircraft suspensions although neither carrier would give a figure.

"A combination of re-scheduling the unaffected seven aircraft A320 fleet and transferring passengers to other carriers aims to ensure that 90 percent of Dragonair travellers should be able to reach their destinations as planned today," Dragonair said in a statement.

Another Cathay spokeswoman said the airline did not aim at putting on replacement aircraft, while the Draganair statement said it was evaluating whether to lease additional aircraft on a short-term basis to offset lost A330 capacity.

The Cathay spokeswoman said the amount of cargoes being affected was insignificant. "There is not a significant amount of cargo being affected at this point in time," she said, declining to disclose their value for "commercial reasons".
The airline had been been helping shippers send their cargoes on other flights unless they wanted to keep them temporarily, she said.
Dragonair gave no information on the impact on cargoes.
Swire Pacific Ltd and Cathay Pacific Airways Ltd together hold about 26 percent of Dragonair, whose major shareholder is China National Aviation Corp.

The two carriers said they took the precaution of suspending A330-300 operations until the engine manufacturer could provide sufficient assurance that the reliability problems of the engine were resolved.
Cathay's engineering director, Rowland Fairfield, said the aircraft could be grounded for weeks.
"It's difficult to predict precisely -- anywhere between a few days and a few weeks," he told local radio.
The airlines said the problem with an engine part in the Rolls-Royce Trent 700 engine had been "clearly identified and understood" and a long-term design solution had been found.
But the design would have to be endurance tested before it could be released for service, the carriers said.
